title: Object Pose Estimation with Statistical Guarantees: Conformal Keypoint Detection and Geometric Uncertainty Propagation
title_audio_script: This paper, from NVIDIA Research and presented at CVPR 2023, tackles a safety-critical gap in object pose estimation: existing two-stage pipelines detect keypoints and solve for the 6D pose, but give no provable guarantee on how wrong the answer might be. The authors inject two changes into that pipeline. Conformal keypoint detection turns heuristic heatmap detections into circular or elliptical prediction sets that provably cover the true keypoints with a user-chosen probability, say ninety percent. Geometric uncertainty propagation then pushes those keypoint sets through the geometry to form a Pose Uncertainty Set, or PURSE, that covers the true pose with the same probability. From PURSE they compute an average pose by random sample averaging, and use semidefinite relaxation to bound the worst-case rotation and translation error. On the LineMOD Occlusion dataset the sets achieve valid coverage, the bounds are correct, and the average pose matches or beats strong baselines.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.necessary: Two-stage object pose estimators (detect keypoints, then solve PnP) perform well on benchmarks but offer no provable guarantee on the quality or uncertainty of the estimated 6D pose.
sections.additional: Safety-critical uses (autonomous driving, robotic manipulation, space robotics) need provably correct estimates with formal worst-case error bounds, which prior pipelines lack.
sections.audio_script: Estimating an object's 6D pose from an image underlies augmented reality, autonomous driving, robotic manipulation, and space robotics. The dominant recipe is a two-stage pipeline: first detect semantic keypoints on the image, then compute the pose by minimizing reprojection error through Perspective-n-Points. These methods score well on standard benchmarks, but they hand back a single pose with no statement about how trustworthy it is. For safety-critical systems that is a serious gap, because there is no provable guarantee on the quality of the keypoints, no guarantee the optimizer found the right pose, and no formal bound on the worst-case error between the estimate and the truth.

sections.heading: Motivation
sections.necessary: Neural keypoint detectors can be arbitrarily wrong (outliers), robust back-ends like RANSAC give no optimality guarantee and can fail silently, and no prior method certifies a worst-case error bound between the estimate and the groundtruth.
sections.additional: Three challenges: (C1) keypoints may be far from groundtruth, (C2) outlier rejection is nonconvex and heuristics lack global optimality, (C3) no provably correct uncertainty quantification exists.
sections.audio_script: Why is this hard? The authors name three challenges. First, keypoints from neural networks can be arbitrarily wrong, producing outliers. Second, the second stage must reject those outliers, which is a nonconvex optimization; fast heuristics like RANSAC are widely used but cannot guarantee global optimality and often fail without notice. Third, and most fundamentally, there is no provably correct uncertainty quantification, meaning no formal worst-case error bound between the estimate and the groundtruth. Recent work could certify global optimality of the optimization, but that still does not deliver a probabilistic guarantee on the pose itself. This paper sets out to provide exactly that guarantee, end to end.

sections.heading: Contribution
sections.necessary: The first object pose estimator endowing an estimate with provable and computable worst-case error bounds, via two additions to the two-stage paradigm: conformal keypoint detection and geometric uncertainty propagation.
sections.additional: Introduces the Pose Uncertainty Set (PURSE), the RANdom SAmple averaGing (RANSAG) sampler for computing an average pose, and semidefinite relaxations that upper-bound the worst-case rotation and translation errors.
sections.audio_script: The core contribution is the first pose estimator that attaches provable and computable worst-case error bounds to its output. It does so with two ingredients. Conformal keypoint detection applies inductive conformal prediction to convert heuristic heatmap detections into circular or elliptical prediction sets that cover the true keypoints with a user-specified marginal probability. Geometric uncertainty propagation then propagates those keypoint constraints to the 6D pose, forming a Pose Uncertainty Set, abbreviated PURSE, that covers the true pose with the same probability. Because PURSE is a nonconvex set, the authors add a sampler called RANSAG to extract an average pose and a semidefinite relaxation to bound the worst-case errors.

sections.heading: Method
sections.necessary: Inductive conformal prediction calibrates heatmap nonconformity scores on a calibration set to build per-keypoint prediction sets (balls or ellipses) with 1−ε coverage. These constraints define the nonconvex PURSE over SE(3); RANSAG samples keypoints, solves P3P/PnP, and averages accepted poses into an average pose. A semidefinite relaxation maximizes pose-to-PURSE distance to certify worst-case rotation and translation bounds.
sections.additional: Two nonconformity designs — peak (scaled peak-to-true error) and covariance (Mahalanobis distance over top-J detections) — yield circular vs elliptical sets. The worst-case bound problem is nonconvex; its SDP relaxation is either exact or gives a valid upper bound.
sections.audio_script: The method works in two stages. In conformal keypoint detection, a calibration set of labeled images is used to compute nonconformity scores for the heatmap detector. The authors offer two score designs: a peak design that measures the scaled distance between the true keypoint and the heatmap's most probable pixel, and a covariance design that measures a Mahalanobis distance over the top detections, giving circular and elliptical prediction sets respectively. Sorting these scores yields a threshold that guarantees each true keypoint lies in its prediction set with probability one minus epsilon. In geometric uncertainty propagation, these keypoint sets become quadratic constraints on the 6D pose, defining the Pose Uncertainty Set. Since that set is nonconvex, RANSAG samples three keypoints at a time, solves the minimal P3P problem, keeps poses inside the set, and averages them into an average pose. Finally, to bound the error, the authors maximize the distance from the average pose to the farthest pose still inside PURSE, relax this nonconvex problem into a semidefinite program, and solve it, producing certified worst-case rotation and translation bounds.

sections.heading: Dataset / Benchmark
sections.necessary: Evaluated on the LineMOD Occlusion (LM-O) dataset: 1214 test images of 8 objects on a table; the 200 BOP-selected images serve as the calibration set and all 1214 images for testing.
sections.additional: Four setups combine detection source (groundtruth or Faster-RCNN bounding boxes) with prediction-set shape (ball or ellipse): gt-ball, gt-ellipse, frcnn-ball, frcnn-ellipse. The dataset's uniform pose sampling supports the exchangeability assumption conformal prediction requires.
sections.audio_script: Experiments run on the LineMOD Occlusion dataset, a standard and challenging benchmark of 1214 test images showing eight objects on a table under heavy occlusion. Two hundred images selected by the BOP challenge are used as the calibration set that conformal prediction needs, and the full set of images is used for testing. The authors evaluate four setups that cross two choices: whether keypoints come from groundtruth bounding boxes or a Faster-RCNN detector, and whether the prediction sets are circular balls or elliptical. They also check the exchangeability assumption that conformal prediction relies on, noting that the dataset was collected with uniform pose sampling rather than a single continuous video, which keeps the assumption plausible.

sections.heading: Key Result
sections.necessary: On LM-O the prediction sets attain their target coverage (empirical coverage near 90% at ε=0.1), the worst-case error bounds are always correct whenever PURSE contains the groundtruth pose, and the average pose matches or beats strong baselines on the 2D-projection success metric.
sections.additional: In the coverage-vs-bound plots, points covered by PURSE (blue circles) never cross the y=x diagonal, confirming the bounds upper-bound the true error as guaranteed with probability 1−ε.
sections.audio_script: The results confirm the theory on all three fronts. First, the conformal prediction sets achieve valid coverage: at a target of ninety percent, the empirical coverage across objects sits right around ninety percent, and it concentrates more tightly as the calibration set grows. Second, the worst-case error bounds are correct: in the scatter plots comparing the certified bound against the actual error, every case where PURSE covers the true pose stays below the diagonal, meaning the bound is never violated when the guarantee holds. Third, the average pose is accurate: judged by the two-dimensional projection metric, it achieves significantly higher success rates than prior methods when using groundtruth bounding boxes, and comparable rates when using Faster-RCNN detections.

sections.heading: Ablation Study
sections.necessary: Varying the error rate ε (0.1 vs 0.4) trades coverage for tightness: larger ε shrinks the prediction sets and improves average-pose success but lowers coverage. Elliptical (covariance) sets generally match or beat circular (ball) sets, and accuracy rises with ε.
sections.additional: A first-order SDP relaxation gives looser but faster bounds than the second-order relaxation; solving the bound for multiple RANSAG samples and taking the minimum slightly tightens the translation bounds (Remark 4).
sections.audio_script: The authors probe several design choices. The error rate epsilon acts as a dial: a smaller epsilon like zero point one gives larger, more conservative prediction sets and stronger coverage, while a larger epsilon like zero point four shrinks the sets and raises the average pose's success rate at the cost of coverage. Elliptical prediction sets, built from the covariance design, generally perform as well as or better than circular ball sets. They also compare relaxation orders: a first-order semidefinite relaxation is faster but yields looser bounds than the second-order relaxation, and computing bounds over several sampled poses and keeping the minimum slightly tightens the translation bounds.

sections.heading: Headline Numbers
sections.necessary: - Target coverage 90% (ε=0.1) is empirically attained on LM-O, with as few as n=200 calibration images. - Average-pose success (2D-projection, <5px error) reaches ~70.6% (gt-ellipse, ε=0.1) versus 61.1% for PVNet, the strongest baseline. - Worst-case bounds are correct in 100% of cases where PURSE covers the groundtruth pose (blue points never cross y=x).
sections.additional: - LM-O: 1214 test images, 8 objects; 200 calibration images. - RANSAG typically returns ~100 valid pose samples with T=1000 trials.
sections.audio_script: A few numbers capture the impact. With a target coverage of ninety percent and a calibration set of just two hundred images, the method empirically meets that coverage on LineMOD Occlusion. On the two-dimensional projection success metric, where a pose counts as correct if its mean reprojection error is under five pixels, the average pose with groundtruth boxes and elliptical sets reaches about seventy point six percent, beating the strongest baseline PVNet at roughly sixty-one percent. And the certified worst-case bounds hold in every single case where the Pose Uncertainty Set actually covers the true pose, exactly the probability-one-minus-epsilon guarantee the theory promises.

sections.heading: Takeaway
sections.necessary: By marrying conformal prediction with geometric uncertainty propagation, the two-stage pose pipeline becomes the first to output an estimate carrying a provable, computable worst-case error bound, without sacrificing accuracy.
sections.additional: The framework is detector-agnostic (wraps any heatmap keypoint network) and points toward statistically guaranteed perception for other geometric vision problems.
sections.audio_script: The lasting message is that you can turn a standard two-stage pose estimator into one that tells you how wrong it might be, with a real statistical guarantee, and pay little to nothing in accuracy. Conformal prediction supplies coverage guarantees on the keypoints, geometry propagates those guarantees to the pose as the Pose Uncertainty Set, and semidefinite relaxation converts the set into concrete worst-case error bounds. Because it wraps any heatmap-based keypoint detector, the approach is broadly applicable, and it opens a path toward provably correct perception for other geometric vision problems where safety matters.
